ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure is square ABCD, with A at the upper left corner, B at the upper right corner, C at the lower right corner, and D at the lower left corner. The square is divided into small squares of 4 rows and 4 columns. Numbering rows from top to bottom and columns from left to right, the small squares that have already been blackened are: (1,1), (1,3), (1,4), (3,4), (4,2). Reasoning: It is required that diagonal BD become the axis of symmetry. BD is the anti-diagonal from the upper right to the lower left, so the symmetric position of small square (r,c) with respect to BD is (5-c,5-r). (1,4) is on BD and does not need pairing; the symmetric square of (1,1) is (4,4), currently white; the symmetric square of (1,3) is (2,4), currently white; the symmetric square of (3,4) is (1,2), currently white; the symmetric square of (4,2) is (3,1), currently white. Therefore these 4 small squares must at least be blackened additionally. After blackening these 4, all black squares are paired with respect to BD or are on BD, so symmetry can be achieved.

raw_record.question_text: What is the minimum number of small squares that must be colored black so that a line of symmetry lies on the diagonal $\overline{BD}$ of square $ABCD$?

method.method_draft: First describe the diagram as a 4 by 4 grid inside square ABCD, with A at the upper left, B at the upper right, C at the lower right, and D at the lower left. Number rows from top to bottom and columns from left to right. From the image, record the currently black small squares: (1,1), (1,3), (1,4), (3,4), and (4,2). The text asks for the fewest additional small squares to color black so that diagonal BD is a line of symmetry. Use reflection across diagonal BD, the anti-diagonal of the grid: a cell (r,c) reflects to (5-c,5-r). Check each existing black square. The square (1,4) lies on BD, so it needs no partner. The other black squares require their reflected partners: (1,1) needs (4,4), (1,3) needs (2,4), (3,4) needs (1,2), and (4,2) needs (3,1). These four partner cells are currently white, so at least 4 squares must be added, and coloring exactly those 4 achieves the symmetry.
